title: Sources and further reading
introHtml: This document draws on established learning-science research. Every link in it was checked when the document was expanded on 8 October 2026. The time-cost estimates are rough practical estimates from typical study practice, not measured values, and the evidence ratings (strong, moderate, limited) are approximate summaries of the research. Links can move over time; if one breaks, searching for the title usually finds the new location.

items.title: Books for students
items.leadHtml:
• Make It Stick by Brown, Roediger and McDaniel (2014): the most readable summary of retrieval, spacing and interleaving. Read it first if you read only one book: it is written for learners, full of stories from students, pilots and surgeons, and explains why the techniques that feel hardest work best. Harvard University Press
  • How We Learn by Benedict Carey (2014): a science journalist's tour of forgetting, sleep, distraction, spacing and interleaving. Good if you want the surprising "why" behind the habits, told as stories rather than as a manual. Penguin Random House
  • A Mind for Numbers by Barbara Oakley (2014), and her free course "Learning How to Learn" on Coursera: practical and encouraging, especially if maths or science feels like "not your thing". It covers focused and diffuse thinking, chunking, procrastination and test preparation. Book page on Barbara Oakley's site · Learning How to Learn on Coursera (free to enrol; Coursera may charge for a certificate)
  • Atomic Habits by James Clear (2018): habit building and identity. Useful for the hardest part of good studying, which is doing it consistently: small habits, cues, habit stacking and "becoming the kind of person who reviews every day". Book page on James Clear's site
  • Deep Work by Cal Newport (2016): focus and distraction. Makes the case for long stretches of undistracted work and gives concrete rules for protecting them from phones, messages and shallow busywork. Cal Newport's books page

items.title: Free websites and courses
items.leadHtml:
• The Learning Scientists: cognitive psychologists who explain six evidence-based strategies (spaced practice, retrieval practice, elaboration, interleaving, concrete examples, dual coding) with free posters, blog posts and a podcast, for students and teachers.
  • Retrieval Practice: Pooja K. Agarwal's site, with short practical guides, research summaries and free downloads. Start with Brain Dump: A small strategy with a big impact.
  • How To Remember Anything Forever-ish: Nicky Case's interactive comic on the forgetting curve, spaced repetition and the Leitner box.
  • Learning How to Learn: Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski's online course on Coursera. Free to enrol, short video lessons with quizzes.
  • Strengthening the Student Toolbox: John Dunlosky's plain-language summary, in American Educator, of which study strategies work and which do not. The most useful ten-minute read for anyone who wants the evidence behind this document.
  • Which Study Strategies Make the Grade?: the Association for Psychological Science's short summary of the Dunlosky et al. (2013) review.
  • Augmenting Long-term Memory: Michael Nielsen's long, thoughtful essay on how he uses Anki to read and understand research papers. For people who want to take spaced repetition beyond vocabulary.

items.title: Key research
items.leadHtml:
The 11 items from the first version, each with the paper behind it:

  • Dunlosky and colleagues (2013), review of ten study techniques: practice testing and distributed practice rated highest; highlighting and re-reading rated low. Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J. & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
  • Roediger and Karpicke (2006): retrieval practice beats re-studying for long-term retention. Roediger, H. L. & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science.
  • Cepeda and colleagues (2006, 2008): spacing effect and optimal review gaps. Cepeda, N. J., Pashler, H., Vul, E., Wixted, J. T. & Rohrer, D. (2006). Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis. Psychological Bulletin. And Cepeda, N. J., Vul, E., Rohrer, D., Wixted, J. T. & Pashler, H. (2008). Spacing effects in learning: A temporal ridgeline of optimal retention. Psychological Science.
  • Bjork and Bjork: desirable difficulties. Bjork, R. A. & Bjork, E. L. (2020). Desirable difficulties in theory and practice. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition.
  • Rohrer and Taylor (2007), Kornell and Bjork (2008): interleaving. Rohrer, D. & Taylor, K. (2007). The shuffling of mathematics problems improves learning. Instructional Science. And Kornell, N. & Bjork, R. A. (2008). Learning concepts and categories: Is spacing the "enemy of induction"?. Psychological Science.
  • Pashler and colleagues (2008): no good evidence for learning styles. Pashler, H., McDaniel, M., Rohrer, D. & Bjork, R. (2008). Learning styles: Concepts and evidence. Psychological Science in the Public Interest.
  • Agarwal and colleagues (2014): retrieval practice and lower test anxiety. Agarwal, P. K., D'Antonio, L., Roediger, H. L., McDermott, K. B. & McDaniel, M. A. (2014). Classroom-based programs of retrieval practice reduce middle school and high school students' test anxiety. Journal of Applied Research in Memory and Cognition.
  • Ramirez and Beilock (2011): expressive writing before exams. Ramirez, G. & Beilock, S. L. (2011). Writing about testing worries boosts exam performance in the classroom. Science.
  • Gollwitzer (1999): implementation intentions. Gollwitzer, P. M. (1999). Implementation intentions: Strong effects of simple plans. American Psychologist.
  • Deci and Ryan: self-determination theory (autonomy, competence, relatedness). Ryan, R. M. & Deci, E. L. (2000). Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being. American Psychologist.
  • Deng, Gluckstein and Larsen (2015): flashcard (Anki) use and medical licensing exam scores. Deng, F., Gluckstein, J. A. & Larsen, D. P. (2015). Student-directed retrieval practice is a predictor of medical licensing examination performance. Perspectives on Medical Education.

Other landmark papers cited in this document:

  • Karpicke, J. D. & Blunt, J. R. (2011). Retrieval practice produces more learning than elaborative studying with concept mapping. Science. Writing down what you remember beat building concept maps with the text open.
  • Kang, S. H. K. (2016). Spaced repetition promotes efficient and effective learning: Policy implications for instruction. Policy Insights from the Behavioral and Brain Sciences. A short, readable overview of spacing for teachers and students.
  • Gollwitzer, P. M. & Sheeran, P. (2006). Implementation intentions and goal achievement: A meta-analysis of effects and processes. Advances in Experimental Social Psychology. "If X, then I will Y" plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals across many studies.
  • Karpicke, J. D., Butler, A. C. & Roediger, H. L. (2009). Metacognitive strategies in student learning: Do students practise retrieval when they study on their own?. Memory. Most students re-read; few test themselves.
  • Szpunar, K. K., Khan, N. Y. & Schacter, D. L. (2013). Interpolated memory tests reduce mind wandering and improve learning of online lectures. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
  • Diekelmann, S. & Born, J. (2010). The memory function of sleep. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.
  • Ophir, E., Nass, C. & Wagner, A. D. (2009). Cognitive control in media multitaskers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
  • Ericsson, K. A., Krampe, R. T. & Tesch-Römer, C. (1993). The role of deliberate practice in the acquisition of expert performance. Psychological Review.

Each section of this document also has its own Further reading boxes with the articles and papers behind its specific items.
